entries.title: Fonts on a mobile profile
entries.lead: A profile claiming a phone reports the fonts that phone has, and none of the machine's own.

blocks.text: A page learns which fonts you have by measuring text, and a phone profile used to measure the fonts of the computer it was running on — a page could find Apple Chancery, or Segoe UI, on a device that has neither. The profile now carries the device's own set, and that set is all a page can find.

Names the device really has answer as present even when the machine has no such file, because the browser draws them with a face it does have. What cannot be reproduced is the exact shape of the letters: the widths are the stand-in's. A detector holding a table of real widths can still tell; one asking which fonts exist cannot.

The set is written as groups, because a phone's font configuration mostly is: on Android, Arial, Helvetica, Tahoma and Verdana are one file, and a page measuring all four gets one width. Android profiles carry their maker's own fonts too — Samsung, Motorola, OnePlus, Xiaomi and vivo each add their own.

entries.title: WebGPU on a Linux profile
entries.lead: A profile claiming Linux gave the machine's own graphics adapter away.

blocks.text: Chrome on Linux ships with WebGPU switched off, so a page asking it for an adapter is answered with nothing. Ours answered with the adapter of the machine it ran on — vendor "apple", architecture "metal-3", beside a WebGL string naming an NVIDIA card on a Mesa driver. It now answers with nothing, the way Chrome on Linux does. navigator.gpu stays where it is; it is the adapter request that comes back empty.

entries.title: Protected video on Android profiles
entries.lead: An optional switch for the video a phone can play and a desktop cannot.

blocks.text: Almost any current phone plays protected video at a level no desktop offers, and a site that checks gets a different answer from a profile claiming a phone. Turn on Media in the profile editor and the profile claims it. It is off by default and only offered on mobile profiles, because the claim is only as good as the machine behind it: a site that takes it up will ask for video this computer may not be able to decode.

entries.title: Turning the screen
entries.lead: A mobile profile can be turned, and everything turns with it.

blocks.text: Over the debugging port, Motion.setOrientation turns the claimed screen. The screen, the window, the media queries a page lays itself out with and the motion sensors all follow — and the sensors travel through the turn the way a hand does rather than jumping, because a device that arrives at a new angle without having moved is not a device.

entries.title: Dragging with a finger
entries.lead: A new step for carrying something across the page, where a swipe only flicks it.

blocks.text: A swipe scrolls; a drag moves the thing under the finger. The finger now rests long enough for the page to decide it is a drag and not a scroll, then travels from where it came to rest — which is what a slider, a map or a sortable list needs. Automation reaches it as Motion.touchDrag, and the launcher's own drag step uses it on a mobile profile.

entries.title: Graphics features in profiles
entries.lead: Profiles carry the WebGPU features of the device they were taken from.

blocks.text: A page can list those features in one call, and a list belonging to a different card than the one the profile names is a contradiction. Every profile in the library now carries its own, and the browser never reports more than the machine can actually back.

Fixed along the way: the warning about a feature your machine cannot provide was shown for every profile at once, because the list of what this machine supports had been recorded before there was anything to record. A missing record is no longer read as "supports nothing".

entries.title: Mobile profile
entries.lead: A profile claiming a phone now reports one consistently: its connection, orientation, fonts and motion sensors all agree with the device it says it is.

blocks.text: The connection block takes raw values now — the ones the device would have measured — and the browser rounds them the way it rounds real ones. A profile pinning 75 ms used to report exactly 75, which no Chrome reports, and the same number to every site. Add "type" to name the link, for example "cellular4g".

Screen orientation follows the screen the profile already sets, so a portrait phone no longer says landscape. There is no separate setting for it, on purpose: a second place to state which way the device is held is how the two ended up disagreeing.

Fonts match what a phone has: the local font list is gone, the decorative generic families collapse onto the default as they do on Android, and text scaling works. Page text may render slightly differently on a mobile profile as a result.

Motion sensors report a device being held. Add "motion": { "carry": "hand" } — or "table" or "walking" — to choose how much it moves. Without them a page listening for movement heard nothing at all, which no phone does.

entries.title: Touch
entries.lead: A profile can now claim a phone, and the browser behaves like one: your mouse and wheel reach the page as finger touches, not as a cursor.

blocks.text: Set the profile's platform or user agent to Android, or turn on the mobile client hint, and the page reports touch points, a coarse pointer and no hovering — the same set a real phone reports.

From then on the wheel scrolls the page by dragging a finger, a click is a tap, dragging is a swipe, and the right button opens the touch context menu by holding. Moving the mouse without a button does nothing at all, because a phone cannot hover.

This changes what you can do by hand: selecting text by dragging works the way it does on a phone, not the way it does on a desktop. Scrolling with a trackpad still carries momentum; scrolling with a notched wheel does not, for the same reason a slow finger drag does not.
Automation gets four steps over the debugging port — tap, hold, swipe and pinch. The pointer steps refuse on a mobile profile and say so, because a phone moving a cursor contradicts itself.

entries.title: Automation
entries.lead: A new section for building and running your own scripts against your profiles.

blocks.text: A project is a list of steps. Add them from a library grouped by what they do — navigation, pointer, keyboard, flow, data — and fill in each step's fields.

Every step says where the run goes next, both when it works and when it does not: on to the next one, jump to another step, try again, end the pass, or stop this profile. Failure stops by default, because carrying on after a click that found nothing is how a run ends up typing into the wrong page.

Open a profile inside the section and its window appears next to the list. Click, type and scroll straight on it. Right-click offers what to do with whatever is under the cursor; shift and right-click opens the page's own menu instead. Turn recording on and everything you do is written down as you go — clicks, keys, scrolling and the pages you open.
Every click and keystroke — yours and the project's — goes through the browser's own human-input engine. A site sees a person moving a mouse, not a script firing events.

Run a project against as many profiles as you like, several at a time, for a number of passes or for a number of hours. The Fleet window shows every browser in the run and which step it is on, and each run keeps its own log on disk.

A project can be exported to a file and imported somewhere else. Any module its steps use goes inside the file, so the project runs where it lands; a module already installed under the same name is kept as it is rather than replaced. Any field you mark as secret is left blank on the way out, and you are told what to fill in on the way back.

You can add your own blocks by writing a small module in Rust. It never touches the page: it is handed the step's settings and answers with ordinary actions the launcher performs itself. Modules are added and removed at the bottom of the Automation section, and the steps they bring sit in the library in a group of their own.

entries.title: Automation from a script
entries.lead: Projects can now be run from outside the app.

blocks.text: Everything the Automation section does — list projects, read one, replace it, run it, see how a run is going, stop it, export and import — now has an address on the launcher's local API, and the MCP server has a tool for each. Until now a project could only be started by hand in the window.
It uses the same token as the rest of the API, from Settings → Automation API. Modules are covered too: list what is installed, add a .wasm from a path on this machine, remove one.

entries.title: Screen scaling
entries.lead: Two ways a page could read the real scaling of your monitor, and one way it could catch the profile out by zooming.

blocks.text: A CSS paint worklet has a screen-scaling number of its own, and it was answering with the machine's, not the profile's. Any page could read it in three lines and no permission is asked for it — next to a window that claimed something else, that is a plain contradiction. The screen-details API, the one behind the window-management permission, gave the real number away the same way, alongside a screen whose width and height were the profile's.

The third one needed no trick at all: on a real machine the reported scaling includes the page's zoom, so it moves the moment you press Ctrl-+. The profile's number stayed put, and a page that compares the window's width against the viewport's could see a page zoomed to 110% still insisting nothing had changed. The zoom is now carried on the profile's number too, so it moves exactly as far as it should. The screen's own figure, which carries no zoom on a real machine either, stays put as it should.

entries.title: Scroll numbers
entries.lead: A page could tell the browser apart by what one turn of the wheel reported.

blocks.text: The window reports the screen scaling its profile claims, and the numbers a wheel produces were being divided by that instead of by the machine's own. One notch arrived as 50 pixels with a wheelDelta of 60, where a real mouse reports 100 and 120 — and a wheelDelta that is not a multiple of 120 is a value no wheel produces. This hit a person scrolling with their own mouse, not only scrolling the browser performs itself.

The division now uses the machine's real scaling, so a notch reports what a notch reports everywhere. The page still reads the profile's scaling from window.devicePixelRatio, unchanged. The correction that used to sit on the browser's own scrolling is gone with it: it straightened only what the browser sent itself, and in synchronised windows it had to be skipped or the copies scrolled twice as far.

entries.title: Arranging browsers on Linux
entries.lead: Windows would not move into place in a Wayland session.

blocks.text: Arranging is each browser putting its own window where it was told, and a Wayland window is not allowed to do that — the request goes nowhere and the desktop places the window as it sees fit. Browsers now start on X11, which inside a Wayland session means XWayland, so arranging works again both in the sync panel and during a run.

Nothing changes if you already log in with Xorg, and your own --ozone-platform in the extra launch arguments still wins. If the session has no X server at all, the browser stays a Wayland window and the automation page now says exactly what that costs — which it used to get wrong, calling everything limited even where arranging was fine. The launcher's own Fleet window still cannot sit above the others under Wayland; nothing in the app can change that.

entries.title: Requests and dragging
entries.lead: Projects can now drag things and send requests of their own.

blocks.text: Dragging was the one gesture missing: the browser could move, click, scroll and type, but not press, carry and let go. It can now — "Drag onto" takes one element to another, and "Swipe" presses and moves by a distance, which is what a slider, a canvas or a sweep that selects text needs. Both travel the same human path as an ordinary movement, and the moves carry the held button, without which a page sees a pointer that merely passed over it.

"Send a request" goes out from the launcher rather than from the page, with a TLS fingerprint you choose — chrome_140, firefox_133, safari_18 and a hundred more — and, by default, through the profile's own proxy, so a call made beside a browsing session comes from the same address. Name a session and cookies and connections carry from one step to the next; leave it empty and the request goes alone. The answer arrives as three names: the body, and beside it the status and the headers.

items: **Waiting**: until an element is gone, until it says something, until the address changes.
**Reading**: how many elements match, an element's attribute, a picture of the page.
**Choosing**: a random number or an item from a list, and a line taken from a file — removed as it is read, so a list of accounts is used once each.

entries.title: Human input over the debugging port
entries.lead: Automated movement and typing failed on every profile started for automation.

blocks.text: The browser only builds its human-input commands when it is told to, and the launcher never told it. Anything driving a profile through the debugging port — the MCP server included — got "command not found" the moment it tried to move the pointer.
It is now switched on whenever a profile is started with the debugging port open. Nothing is added to what a page can see.

entries.title: Window size on Windows and Linux
entries.lead: Profiles opened in a window smaller than the monitor, and maximising did nothing.

blocks.text: A profile carries the screen of the machine its fingerprint was taken from, and the browser both sizes the window to that screen and refuses to let the window grow past it. A profile created on another machine, or added through the API, therefore opened small on a bigger monitor, and pressing maximise only moved the window to the middle of the screen.

On Windows and Linux the screen is now taken from the monitor in front of you every time a profile starts, not only when the profile is created, so the window opens at the size of the desktop and maximises normally. macOS still uses the screen from the fingerprint, unless the real display is smaller than it claims. Settings → Screen resolution set to Real reports the host monitor on every system.

entries.title: Synchronised windows
entries.lead: You work in one window; every other window in the group repeats the same actions in its own profile.

blocks.text: Pointer, keystrokes, scrolling, opening and closing tabs, extension popups. It is not a recording played back: each window performs the action with its own motor profile, so the windows never move identically.
There is no leader to appoint. Whichever window you are typing in is the one driving, because it is the one receiving real input. Switch windows and it follows.

The fill helper is deliberately excluded. In a group every window fills the same form at the same moment with its own generated person, so mirroring those keystrokes would put one window's answers into everyone else's fields.

Fixed: a window that came up zoomed, full-screen or minimised ignored the layout, because in those states the window state owns the geometry. It now leaves that state first. The chosen layout is also remembered, so a profile that finishes starting after the others is placed too.

Fixed: a tab opened by a site — `target=_blank` or `window.open` — stayed behind in the other windows when it was closed. Such tabs are never broadcast, since every window opens its own from the same mirrored click, so there was no name to close by. They now get a name both sides work out independently, and the close carries the page address as a check, so a window that finds something else under that name leaves it alone.

entries.title: Human typing in the browser
entries.lead: Right-click a field and the browser types into it the way a person does.

blocks.text: The context menu of any text field, search box or `contenteditable` gets two entries: **Human Type**, which types the clipboard, and **Fill with generated**, a submenu of eight values generated for this profile — name, surname, email, username, phone and the rest. Each entry shows the value it will type.
The text is not set on the element and not pasted. It goes in key by key, through the same path a keyboard uses:

items: gaps between keystrokes vary instead of being a fixed delay
timing depends on the letter pair — `th` is faster than `qz`, as it is for a person
keys overlap: the next goes down before the previous comes up
a per-character bias that belongs to the profile and survives restarts
optional typos, made and corrected with a real backspace

blocks.text: The pointer moves the same way, with overshoot and correction, and takes longer to reach a small target than a large one. Password fields are excluded.
No JavaScript is injected. The whole path is C++ inside the browser process, so a page cannot detect a script that was never there.

entries.title: Human typing over CDP
entries.lead: The same typing and pointer engine, driven from a script.

blocks.text: The commands live in a `Motion` domain on the browser target. It does not appear in `/json/protocol` or `Schema.getDomains`, and the command names deliberately do not match those of other automation tools.

Create the pointer first: a session without one answers every other command with an error rather than guessing where the cursor is, since a guessed starting point gives the wrong duration and the wrong curve. Pass the element's real width as `targetWidth` — that is what makes the timing believable.
Worked example in the README, section “Human input over CDP”.

entries.title: Camera
entries.lead: The profile has a camera even on a machine that has none, and it shows the photo or video you pick.

blocks.text: The machine's camera list is replaced, not added to. A page never reaches the real camera — which matters because the profile's fingerprint already names a specific camera model, and handing over the host's would contradict it.

Pick the file from the control left of the app menu while the browser is running. PNG, JPEG, MP4, MOV, WebM, Y4M and MJPEG are accepted, and the format is detected from the file's contents, so a wrong extension does not matter. Video loops, so a short clip is enough.

The panel shows the first frame with a selection rectangle: drag inside it to move, drag a corner to resize, and the numbers beside it let you write a framing down and repeat it. The rectangle keeps the camera's aspect ratio, so the picture is never stretched or letterboxed. For a portrait or square photo there is a checkbox that fits the whole image instead and fills the space beside it.
What a page gets is a camera, not a file:

items: the device name and id are the profile's, not the path to your file
a normal ladder of resolutions, not just the one the picture happens to be
pan, tilt and zoom crop the picture for real, and are reported as supported only when the model the profile claims has them
frames carry sensor noise, so no two are identical — a page comparing consecutive frames does not see a frozen image
frame timing has a millisecond or two of jitter, as real hardware does

blocks.text: With nothing picked the camera still works and shows a dark frame, rather than failing. A camera that enumerates and then never delivers is itself detectable.

entries.title: Form filling helper
entries.lead: The browser finds the fields, offers them, and fills them on one button.

blocks.text: Enabled per profile. The browser watches the page, offers the fields it can fill, and on one press types them in one at a time. Generated identities are stable per profile: the profile is the account, and an account has one owner.
Three sources are used, each answering one question:

items: **Autofill** — what a field is: a first name, a year of birth, a gender.

**The accessibility tree** — whether the element is still there, where, and whether it is shown. Read fresh several times over the first seconds of a step, and matched by element id rather than position, because two steps of one signup can occupy the same rectangle.

**Focus after the click** — whether the click landed. Nothing in the browser process knows what is painted on top of what, so if another element took the focus the field is skipped instead of typed into blind.

blocks.text: Drop-downs built from a `div` and a `ul`, which autofill cannot see, are found through the accessibility tree and filled by clicking the box and then the option.

Fixed: a signup that swapped its step inside one document left the helper offering the previous step's fields, so filling put a name into the date row. Three causes: the old step stayed in autofill's cache, the old fields were laid out underneath the new ones at the same coordinates, and a step that starts hidden was parsed once at load with every field marked unfocusable and never re-read. The accessibility tree now settles all three.
The offer also settles itself: the page is looked at several times over the first seconds of a step, so a half-parsed form corrects itself instead of waiting for you to touch something.

entries.title: Human input in MCP
entries.lead: The Motion domain wrapped so a model can aim at an element instead of a coordinate.

blocks.text: The bundled MCP server gains `human_click`, `human_move`, `human_fill` and `human_type`. They take the same selectors as the existing browser tools; the wrapper resolves the element, scrolls it into view and passes the core its coordinates together with the element's real width, which is what makes a small target take longer to reach.

human_fill(profile_id, "#email", "ada@example.com")
human_fill(profile_id, "#email", "new@…", clear: true)
human_click(profile_id, "button[type=submit]")

`clear` selects the current value with a triple click rather than a keyboard shortcut, so the clearing is as human as the typing. Give `x` and `y` instead of a selector when the coordinates are already known. The calls take real time and report how long the move and the typing took.

entries.title: Per-profile window icon
entries.lead: Each profile's window shows its own name and colour.

blocks.text: In the Dock, the taskbar and Alt-Tab you see which profile you are switching to. The name is set as large as it fits, wrapping to at most three lines; a name too long to fit is trimmed with an ellipsis.
The icon is shaped the way each system shapes its own: a squircle with a shadow on macOS, a full-bleed rounded square on Windows, an Adwaita outline on Linux.
Nothing to set up. Rename a profile and its icon follows on the next launch.

entries.title: Profile colour
entries.lead: One colour per profile, on its window icon and behind its name in the omnibox.

blocks.text: Pick it in the profile editor. The window icon takes it, and so does the pill carrying the profile's name in the omnibox, so the two never disagree about which profile you are looking at.

Left on **Auto** the icon derives a colour from the name — the same profile always the same colour, and the thing you can still tell apart at 32 px — while the pill keeps the browser's own toolbar colour and follows the theme.
`color` is a field on profile create and edit, so a scripted fleet can come out colour-coded.

entries.title: Extension library
entries.lead: Add an extension once, then pick it per profile.

blocks.text: **Library → Extensions** → *From link*: give it a Web Store address and the extension downloads itself. Pasting just the id out of the address works too, as does a direct link to a `.crx` or `.zip`. A file or an unpacked folder can be added the same way.

Each one shows its name, version, description and icon, read out of the extension itself — so what the grid shows is what the browser will load. In the profile editor they are chips: tick the ones this profile should run, and different profiles can carry different sets.
Removing an extension from the library stops every profile loading it from its next start; profiles hold a reference, not a copy.
Also over the API and MCP: `POST /extensions` takes the same link, and a profile's `extensions` is a field on create and edit.

entries.title: Folder bookmarks
entries.lead: A site bound to a folder appears in the bookmarks bar of every profile in that folder.

blocks.text: **Library → Bookmarks**: add a site, pick the folder. Every profile in that folder gets it in a bookmarks-bar folder called **ShardX**, from its next launch. Bound to no folder means every profile.
Only that folder is managed. Bookmarks saved inside a profile are left alone, and a site removed here disappears from the profiles on their next launch.
Also over the API and MCP: `GET`/`POST /bookmarks`.

entries.title: Trash
entries.lead: A deleted profile is kept for 7 days and can be restored with its cookies and logins.

blocks.text: Deleting a profile now moves it to **Trash**, restorable for seven days. What comes back is the account — cookies, saved logins, site data, preferences, history and bookmarks — under the same id, so anything that referenced the profile still points at it.
Caches are not kept, which is why a profile that took a gigabyte sits in the trash as a few megabytes. Deleting a folder together with its profiles goes through the trash too.
After seven days it is gone. **Empty trash** does it sooner.
Also over the API and MCP: `DELETE /profiles/{id}` archives, `GET /trash` lists, `POST /trash/{id}/restore` brings it back.

entries.title: Profile data location
entries.lead: Move profiles, extensions and the trash to another folder or disk.

blocks.text: **Settings → Profile data location** → *Change…* and pick a folder on any disk. Moving shows a progress bar; nothing in the old folder is deleted until every file has arrived and been checked, so a failure part-way leaves you exactly where you were.
Profiles cannot be launched while the move runs — including from the API, so a script cannot start a browser mid-move. Close every running profile first.
A disk mounted read-only is refused before anything is copied, rather than half-way through.

entries.title: Extra launch arguments
entries.lead: Switches added to every profile launch.

blocks.text: **Settings → Extra launch arguments**, one per line or space-separated; quote a value containing spaces. They are applied last, so a switch here also overrides the launcher's own.
Put anything that changes what a page can measure in the profile instead. A switch applied to every profile at once makes them all alike.

entries.title: Proxy names
entries.lead: `host:port:user:pass #facebook` — what follows the hash is the proxy's name.

blocks.text: The name is shown first in the profile's proxy list and in the proxy table, with the address after it. Set it when creating or editing a proxy, or write it into the line you paste. Bulk import reads it and export writes it back.
Leave the name empty and the field's placeholder shows the address it will fall back to. The country is not something you write down — the proxy test fills it in.

entries.title: Distributing proxies
entries.lead: Select proxies, press Distribute, check the pairing, bind.

blocks.text: The dialog puts the two lists side by side and pairs them by position — proxy #1 to profile #1 — so you can check the pairing before binding. One proxy per profile: if the proxies run out, the remaining profiles are left alone rather than sharing an IP.
It applies to profiles **without a proxy** by default. Switch it to all profiles to reassign existing ones; it shows how many bindings would be replaced before you confirm.

entries.title: Adding a proxy from the profile editor
entries.lead: Add and bind a proxy from the profile's own proxy list.

blocks.text: **Create new proxy** sits at the top of the profile's proxy list — the place you are already looking when you find the proxy you wanted is not there. Paste one line and it is read the way bulk import reads it: `host:port`, `host:port:user:pass`, `user:pass@host:port` or a `socks5://` URL, with a trailing `#name`.
What was understood is shown before anything is saved. Saving adds it to the proxy list and binds it to the profile you are editing.

entries.title: Row selection and filters
entries.lead: Shift-click selects a run of rows; filters narrow the profile list.

blocks.text: Shift-click spans from the last row you clicked to the one you shift-click, on both the profiles and the proxies table, and anywhere on the row rather than only the checkbox.
The row you shift-click decides the direction: an unticked row ticks the whole run, a ticked one clears it. That is also how a run selected by mistake is undone.
Profiles filter by whether they are running, by the country of the bound proxy and by whether there is a proxy at all. The button carries a count so you can see when a filter is hiding something.

entries.title: Noise for temporary profiles
entries.lead: `POST /profiles/temporary` takes a noise block.

blocks.text: A temporary profile can now set noise per vector instead of taking the default, which is everything off:

`true` turns a vector on with the strength the UI uses; a full block sets the details. A vector you leave out stays off. The same argument reaches the bundled MCP server as `create_temporary_profile`'s `noise`.
Leave `seed` out. Two temporary profiles created a second apart still get different fingerprints.

entries.title: Fixes
entries.lead: Two places where the launcher's lists were out of date.

items: **A proxy added on the Proxies page was missing from the profile editor** until the app was restarted. It appears immediately now, and a proxy bound by the distribute dialog shows up in the profiles table the same way.
**Country, region and city in the ProxyShard residential generator had no search.** They are searchable now, as is the location picker on the buy card.

entries.title: Engine update detection
entries.lead: A rebuilt engine now reaches you even when the Chromium version has not changed.

blocks.text: The update check only compared Chromium versions, so a second engine build on the same version — new patches, same upstream, which is most releases — was never offered. Three things now say an engine has moved: the Chromium version, the build stamp the release carries, and the archive itself.

A release can also state the launcher version it needs. When it wants a newer one than you are running, the engine update is held back and the launcher update is what you are told about instead — a browser the launcher cannot configure looks like a broken profile rather than a missed update.

entries.title: Patch log after an update
entries.lead: Opens automatically on the first run after an update.

blocks.text: Shown once per version. After that the app opens where it always did.
